MARTINSBURG — Federal authorities continue to investigate a case which an employee of the Bureau of Alcohol Tobacco Firearms and Explosives’ Martinsburg disposal facility allegedly stole a “substantial” number of firearms and gun parts.

Christopher Lee Yates, 52, has been charged in the U.S. District Court of the Northern District of West Virginia on charges of theft of government property and possession of a stolen firearm.

Yates was a contract security guard assigned to the ATF’s National Disposal Branch in Martinsburg, according to April Langwell, chief of the ATF public affairs division.

The allegations surfaced after a Pennsylvania law enforcement partner ran a non-urgent trace on a firearm, Langwell said Thursday. A specific part of the firearm came back to a retired ATF service firearm that was to have been destroyed at the Martinsburg facility.

On March 1, a search of Yates’ vehicle allegedly yielded a firearm concealed in a book bag on the front passenger seat floorboard, according to Federal Court records.

Documents said the firearm was identified as a FNH, model Five-Seven pistol. After a search of ATF records, it was confirmed that the firearm was listed as disposed from the ATF National Firearms Act Division in August 2017, thus confirming it was unlawfully removed from the ATF NFAD facility.

On Feb. 25, in Berkeley County, Yates is alleged to have stolen firearm parts and traveled to Maryland to sell them for financial gain, court records said. The sold firearm slides and firearm parts value exceeded $1,000.

The complaint alleges Yates made an admission to ATF agents that he knowingly was in possession of stolen government property and transferred it to an individual in Maryland on Feb. 25.

According to a statement released by the ATF to The Journal Thursday, authorities immediately launched a criminal investigation and “quickly” identified the suspect.

“ATF immediately launched both a criminal and internal affairs investigation in conjunction with the Department of Justice Office of the Inspector General,” the statement said. “The firearms parts included slides and barrels from retired ATF service weapons.”

Other items unlawfully removed from the facility included firearms and ammunition.

“ATF has made substantial progress in recovering the stolen property and is working around-the-clock to pursue all leads,” according to the statement.

The matter remains under investigation and is being prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Office in the Northern District of West Virginia.

“The Department of Justice and the ATF do not tolerate theft or other violations of law by employees or contractors and will ensure these allegations are thoroughly investigated and take appropriate action against anyone engaging in unlawful behavior,” the statement said.

On March 6, Yates was released from the Eastern Regional Jail with the conditions that he reside with his wife, he follow a curfew and be home 7 p.m. to 7 a.m and he have all firearms and weapons removed from the home prior to his arrival by someone else, according to information discussed at a bond hearing. Yates is scheduled for a preliminary hearing on March 20 in Martinsburg.

U.S. Sens. Ron Johnson, R-WI, and Gary Peters, D-MI, chairman and ranking member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, sent a bipartisan letter to ATF Deputy Director Thomas Brandon requesting information into the case, according to a press release sent Wednesday.

In the letter, the senators seek to understand the “magnitude of the possible threat to public safety, and what the ATF is doing to ensure the situation is properly addressed.”

The letter alleges sources and media have said the theft involves approximately 600 firearm parts. However, Langwell said the ATF is not providing numbers, but have confirmed that the theft was “substantial.”
